text: Paris was under siege and starving, and one bright January morning Monsieur Morissot was walking sadly along the boulevard with an empty stomach. <break time="0.8s" /> A watchmaker with nothing to do in wartime, he walked on slowly, his hands deep in the pockets of his uniform trousers. <break time="0.8s" /> Suddenly he stopped in front of a man whom he recognized at once, for it was Monsieur Sauvage, his old friend from the riverside. <break time="0.8s" /> Before the war, Morissot had left home at dawn every Sunday, with a bamboo rod in his hand and a tin box on his back. <break time="0.8s" /> He took the train to Colombes and walked to the little island of Marante, where he would happily fish until night. <break time="0.8s" /> Every Sunday he met there a stout, cheerful little man, Monsieur Sauvage, who sold cloth in a shop in Paris. <break time="0.8s" /> They often spent half the day side by side, rod in hand and feet hanging over the water, and they became close friends. <break time="0.8s" /> On some days they did not speak at all, for they understood each other perfectly without words, having the same simple tastes. <break time="0.8s" /> On spring mornings, with the warm sun on their backs, Morissot would say, How pleasant this is, and Sauvage would answer, I know nothing better.
